The Container Network Interface is a standard specification (and set of plugins) defining how network interfaces are set up for containers - it's what actually assigns Pod IPs, sets up routing so Pods can reach each other cluster-wide, and implements NetworkPolicy enforcement. Kubernetes itself doesn't implement networking; it delegates to whichever CNI plugin (Calico, Cilium, GKE's native VPC-native networking) is installed on the cluster.
Which CNI have you worked on?: Answer with the actual plugin used (GKE's native VPC-native CNI, Calico, Cilium) and one concrete operational detail - whether NetworkPolicies were actually enforced (not all CNIs enforce them by default - some require a specific plugin like Calico for policy enforcement even on managed platforms), or any networking issue you've debugged at the CNI level.
Do you have experience with a Service Me: Answer honestly with actual scope - which mesh (Istio, Linkerd), whether you configured it yourself (mTLS, traffic splitting, retries/circuit breaking policies) or operated within a mesh someone else set up, since service mesh experience ranges widely in depth.
Can you explain what a Service Mesh is?: A service mesh is an infrastructure layer (typically sidecar proxies injected alongside each service, like Istio's Envoy sidecars) that handles service-to-service concerns - mTLS encryption and identity, traffic management (canary splits, retries, circuit breaking), and observability (automatic metrics/tracing for every request) - without requiring each service to implement these concerns in its own application code.
What is the difference between a Deploym: A Deployment manages interchangeable, stateless replica Pods - any replica can be replaced by an identical new one with no stable identity required. A StatefulSet is for workloads needing stable network identity and per-replica persistent storage (databases, queues) - each replica gets a predictable name and its own PersistentVolumeClaim that persists across restarts, and replicas are created/scaled/deleted in a defined order rather than in parallel.
How do Liveness and Readiness probes dif: A liveness probe checks if the container is still functioning - failure triggers a restart, since a stuck process needs to be killed and restarted to recover. A readiness probe checks if the container is ready to serve traffic - failure removes the Pod from Service endpoints (no traffic routed) without restarting it, letting an app signal 'temporarily busy/starting up' without an unnecessary restart.
What is a Sidecar container?: A secondary container running alongside the main application container within the same Pod, sharing its network namespace and optionally storage volumes - used for cross-cutting concerns like a service mesh proxy (Envoy), a log shipper, or a config-reloader, keeping that concern's logic decoupled from the main application's code while still tightly coupled to its lifecycle.
What is an Ingress Controller?: The actual component (e.g. NGINX Ingress Controller, GKE's Gateway) that watches for Ingress resources in the cluster and configures its underlying proxy/load balancer to implement the routing rules they declare - an Ingress resource by itself does nothing without a controller actively watching and acting on it.
How do you handle Pod Autoscaling?: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler adjusts replica count based on a metric (CPU/memory via metrics-server, or custom request-based metrics via an adapter) relative to a target utilization, within configured min/max bounds - paired with Cluster Autoscaler to ensure enough node capacity exists to actually schedule the additional replicas HPA decides to create.
What is a Kubernetes Secret?: An object storing sensitive data (passwords, API keys, certificates) as base64-encoded key-value pairs, injectable into Pods as environment variables or mounted volumes - base64 is encoding, not encryption, so production setups typically layer on encryption at rest and often an external secrets integration (External Secrets Operator, Sealed Secrets) rather than relying on the Secret object alone for protection.
What is BusyBox?: A single small executable bundling minimal versions of many common Unix utilities (ls, cat, grep, sh, etc.) into one tiny binary - commonly used as a lightweight base image for debug/init containers in Kubernetes (e.g. `kubectl run debug --image=busybox -it -- sh`) when you need basic shell tools without the overhead of a full OS image.
What does etcd store?: The complete state of the Kubernetes cluster - every object's specification and status: Pods, Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets, Namespaces, RBAC bindings, and more. It's the single source of truth the API server reads from and writes to; nothing else in the cluster stores authoritative state anywhere else.
Does etcd store namespaces and storage c: Yes - Namespace objects themselves, along with StorageClass, PersistentVolume, and PersistentVolumeClaim objects (the Kubernetes-level metadata about storage) are all stored in etcd like any other API object. Note that etcd stores the Kubernetes object definitions, not the actual data inside a PersistentVolume itself - that data lives on the actual underlying storage (a cloud disk, NFS), separate from etcd entirely.
What is the use of Helm?: Helm is Kubernetes' package manager - it templates a set of Kubernetes manifests (a chart) with configurable values, letting the same chart be installed multiple times with different configuration (per environment, per tenant) instead of maintaining separate raw YAML per case, and tracks release history so `helm rollback` can revert to a previous release with one command.
What is the difference between AWS VPC,: Conceptually equivalent - each is an isolated virtual network within that cloud for your resources. Key differences: GCP VPCs are global by default (subnets span regions within one VPC, unlike AWS/Azure where the network construct is regional), and default connectivity/firewall models differ slightly (AWS uses Security Groups + NACLs, Azure uses NSGs, GCP uses VPC firewall rules) - the underlying concepts (subnets, route tables, peering) map closely across all three, just with provider-specific terminology and defaults.
How do you connect on-premises resources: A site-to-site VPN (IPsec tunnel over the internet, faster to set up, variable latency) for moderate bandwidth needs, or a dedicated private connection (AWS Direct Connect, Azure ExpressRoute, GCP Cloud Interconnect) for high-bandwidth, low-latency, more reliable connectivity at higher cost - the choice depends on required bandwidth, latency sensitivity, and budget.
How many Kubernetes clusters do you requ: This depends on isolation requirements, not a fixed number - common patterns are one cluster per environment (dev/staging/prod) as a minimum, sometimes further split by region for latency/DR, or by team/business unit for stronger blast-radius isolation - the answer should reason from the actual isolation/compliance/blast-radius needs rather than citing an arbitrary count.
How does a Load Balancer distribute traf: Via weighted traffic splitting - configuring the load balancer (or, in Kubernetes, tools like Istio VirtualServices or Argo Rollouts) with a weight per backend/version (e.g. 50/50 between two Service versions), where the LB probabilistically routes each incoming request according to those weights - commonly used for canary releases or A/B testing between two versions of a service.

What is Terraform State?: A JSON file Terraform maintains mapping your configuration's resources to real-world infrastructure IDs and their last-known attributes - it's what lets `terraform plan` compute an accurate diff against reality without re-querying every attribute from the provider API on every run, and is the mechanism by which Terraform knows what it manages.
Why is Terraform State a security risk?: State files often contain sensitive data in plaintext - resource attributes that happen to include secrets (a database password set as a resource argument, a generated private key) get stored as-is in state, even if marked `sensitive` in configuration (which only redacts CLI output, not the state file itself) - so anyone with read access to the state file/backend can potentially see these values, making state storage access control and encryption at rest essential.
How do you manage state locking in a tea: Use a remote backend with native locking support (GCS backend with its locking mechanism, or Terraform Cloud/Enterprise) so that when one person runs `apply`, a lock is acquired and any concurrent `apply` from someone else blocks until the first completes - preventing two simultaneous applies from corrupting state or making conflicting changes.
When should you use a Terraform Module?: When a set of resources is deployed repeatedly with variation (e.g. the same network/IAM pattern needed per environment or per team) - a module packages that pattern once with clear inputs/outputs, so it's consumed rather than copy-pasted. For a one-off, non-repeated set of resources, a module adds unnecessary abstraction overhead versus just writing the resources directly.
How do you handle secret injection in Te: Source secrets from a secrets manager (GCP Secret Manager, Vault) via a data source at apply time rather than hardcoding them in variables/tfvars, mark sensitive variables/outputs with `sensitive = true` to redact them from CLI output (while remembering this doesn't encrypt the state file itself, which still needs access control), and inject CI/CD-provided secrets as environment variables rather than committing them anywhere in the repo.
What is idempotency in Ansible?: Idempotency means running the same playbook multiple times against the same target produces the same end state without unintended side effects or errors on repeat runs - Ansible modules are designed to check current state first and only make a change if the target doesn't already match the desired state, which is what makes it safe to re-run a playbook repeatedly rather than only being safe to run once.
